scope: Official publisher page and supplied Apollo excerpt, not the full book. Printed page numbers are zine pagination. Historical measurements are dated, not current values.

homepage.title: Can investors lose while useful capacity grows?
homepage.body: Boom argues that concentrated ambition and funding can accelerate innovation. Track two outcomes separately: financial losses and capabilities that remain useful. For AI, compare financial exposure with useful output, sustained usage and infrastructure utilization. Lower prices can help customers while squeezing suppliers. Productive progress alone does not justify a valuation.
homepage.claimType: First sentence: publisher/author thesis. Remaining copy: dashboard inference.

appendix.text: The supplied Boom excerpt examines Apollo as a publicly financed social bubble: political enthusiasm enabled costly overinvestment, while support later faded (zine pp. 19–21). The authors argue NASA procurement accelerated semiconductor affordability and diffusion, while acknowledging those technologies might otherwise have emerged later (pp. 30–31). They also discuss cultural legacy beyond measurable returns (pp. 32–33). These are the authors’ interpretations, not proof that every bubble produces net benefits.

The excerpt does not establish an inflection-versus-mean-reversion taxonomy. The two-column dashboard lens is our inference: trace financial exposure separately from surviving assets, adoption and useful output. Apollo appropriations expose public resources to opportunity cost; that financing differs from shareholder-funded technology firms.

Use dated observations with their original units. Capacity, adoption and falling unit cost are different indicators, so do not combine them into a social-value score. None identifies the counterfactual: what would have happened without excessive investment.

cases.name: AI
cases.lossRisk: Prospective exposure: equity investors, creditors and compute counterparties may bear losses if revenue disappoints. Company financing and compute commitments establish exposure, not realized losses.
cases.lossRiskClaimType: scenario inference from existing verified disclosures
cases.productiveEvidence: GPT-3.5-level inference cost fell more than 280-fold, November 2022–October 2024.
cases.uncertainty: Benchmark-matched inference cost is not full task cost, profitability or current infrastructure utilization.

cases.name: British railways, including Ireland
cases.lossRisk: The promotion boom’s expansion was associated with deteriorating shareholder value.
cases.lossRiskClaimType: paper finding; not quantified loss allocation
cases.productiveEvidence: Open railway mileage rose from 2,343 in 1845 to 6,308 in 1850.
cases.uncertainty: Physical capacity does not establish utilization or net welfare. This is Britain and Ireland, not the U.S. 1873 railway case.

cases.name: Dotcom
cases.lossRisk: Shareholders bore falling equity values; Mishkin distinguishes this episode from bubbles accompanied by marked bank deterioration.
cases.productiveEvidence: U.S. high-speed internet lines grew from about 7.1 million in December 2000 to 9.6 million in June 2001.
cases.uncertainty: An adoption count during the bust does not measure telecom asset utilization, survivor profits or economy-wide net benefit.

evidenceCandidates.label: Inference cost at GPT-3.5-level performance
evidenceCandidates.presentation: Single dated comparison; do not interpolate a monthly cost curve
evidenceCandidates.limits: Published 2025 historical comparison, not a September 2026 quote; benchmark performance is not every useful task.

evidenceCandidates.label: Railway miles open, including Ireland
evidenceCandidates.presentation: Two observations or a chart labeled selected annual observations; no invented monthly values
evidenceCandidates.limits: Stock of physical track, not utilization. Do not mix with England-only figures. Table passenger counts and receipts have period footnotes and are excluded.

evidenceCandidates.label: U.S. high-speed internet lines
evidenceCandidates.limits: Over 200 Kbps in at least one direction, homes and businesses; lines are not unique people. Source growth uses underlying unrounded values, so do not replace its 36% with arithmetic from rounded endpoints.

design.layout: Two parallel columns: financial exposure and observed productive evidence; actual units and dates. Expandable source notes.
prohibitedClaims: No claim productive value offsets an investor loss dollar for dollar
No U.S. railway mapping for British evidence
No monthly values interpolated from endpoints
stillMissing: Comparable AI utilization and useful task cost over time
Residual equipment value and remaining economic asset life
Causal net welfare estimate including opportunity cost and harms
